While not all problems will be as easy to localize and isolate, many will be.

Ensuring that S1 is in the closed (ON) position we then measure the voltage at pin 7 of U1, the audio amplifier. The reading there is 2.5 volts. Since the only component between those two pins is the switch (S1), we can determine that S1 is not operational.
THRESHOLD
Incorrect levels on those pins will affect the entire IC. Looking first at pin 7 of U2B, we measure .01 VDC. This is the voltage that should be seen at the output when a signal is present.

In order to analyze the circuit, we can take some DC measurements. Because the squelch comparator is a part of the same IC as the channel detector, which is functioning, it is not necessary to check Vcc and GND.
Having localized the problem down to five or six components, it's time to isolate the one that's bad.

Further, if an output line is shorted to ground, odds are the IC fried in the process. In either case, the IC will need to be replaced. Because this is a training exercise, troubleshooting different sections of an IC is a reasonable and even desirable endeavor.
If the signal is entering an IC but there is no output, either the output line is shorted to ground or the IC is bad.
In most instances, troubleshooting IC's requires nothing more than comparing outputs against inputs.
In real world practical applications, troubleshooting pins associated with different sections within a single IC may or may not be time and/or money justifiable.
At this point, we have localized the problem to a stage specific area of the PC130-446 card by doing nothing more than being observant and applying a little deductive reasoning.
Since the channel detect light is working, U2A, R4, and R12 are operational. That leaves U2B, R5, R6, C7 and the switch S1, suspect. One other possibility is that pin 7 of U1 (the AF amp) is open.
THRESHOLD
Referring to the schematic of the PC130-446 card we can see that there is very little circuitry remaining that hasn't already been ruled out.

On the assumption that the above determination is true, that leaves the problem located on the PC130-446 card. During the assessment we were able to get voice from the speaker. This tells us that the AF amplifier is working.
Based upon the results, you can determine with a reasonable amount of certainty that the Transceiver is fully operational except for the Squelch.

The seasoned troubleshooter knows that all of these factors come into play when trying to solve a problem. It will not come as a shock to him or her that a suspect component is not the culprit at all.
Compounding this problem, our decisions and actions that follow are often based on those perceptions. It must be assumed then, that how we see something is at least as important as how it really is.

Because all of us think differently, how we perceive something might be radically in opposition to how the same thing is perceived by someone else. All the while, the perceptions of both may be false.
It is for this reason that the creative side of the brain must also be heavily engaged. The best troubleshooters are those that are able to exercise both modes of thought.

Because electronics is based on mathematics, using the logical side of the brain for troubleshooting is imperative. At the same time, a particular symptom may be caused by any number of reasons, many of which will not seem logical at all.

Troubleshooting is a multifaceted process that involves theoretical knowledge, test equipment competency, and understanding the equipment operation, all blended together with a little bit of intuition.
